course_description: Audiences rely exponentially on digital content creators as their primary source of news and information. Audio stories resonate with audiences looking for authenticity, spontaneity and depth. This provides opportunities for students to respond to these demands journalistically in the audio medium via the production of reliable information and content that reaches audiences and supports society. In this subject, students learn how to find, record, structure, produce and edit audio stories for radio and podcast audiences. Using radio and audio theory and traditions as a platform, this course explores a range of audio genres, from radio news to conversational and documentary audio. Students would learn to: interview for sound; record for immersive experience and soundscape; write and script for audio; present and narrate; edit layered audio narratives; and publish and distribute on-demand audio. This is a very practical course, and regular attendance (supplemented with production workshops offered by MaPS) will be important in staying on track with assessments.

course_aims: This course aims to provide you with the fundamental skills and experience in the practice of audio journalism.

learning_outcomes.description: Conceptualise, research and produce audio stories and podcasts by applying a range of journalistic reporting methods.
Demonstrate competency in industry standard technical equipment and production platforms to create audio outputs.
Respond journalistically in the provision of professional content creation using reliable, creative and ethical information gathering judgements.
Critically analyse journalistic practices using relevant theories while exploring a range of audio genres, from radio news to conversational and documentary audio.
Work collaboratively in production teams to plan, produce, and critique audio journalism stories.

assessment_details.title: Short news story
assessment_details.task_description: Students will complete this assignment in groups assigned at the start of the course. Full details will be posted on Blackboard in Week 2. Based on any news of the day, each group will identify and plan a news angle, write a script, and produce a short audio news package for a hypothetical local radio station. The finished story must run 30–45 seconds (target: 40 seconds) and include one soundbite or quote from a source. The following is what is expected for this assignment: Pitch: In your tutorial, pitch your story idea to the class as a group. Research and sourcing: Conduct background research, identify a source, and record a quote (a group member may serve as the source if appropriate) Scripting and voicing: Write the script and assign one group member to voice and record it. Editing: Combine the narration and the soundbite into a single 30–45-second audio story, edited in Audition, and exported as an MP3. The final story should match the format and tone of a commercial or public broadcast news bulletin. Along with the finished audio file, submit your written script. The radio story package will be edited using Audition software. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.task_description: This is an independent assignment, not undertaken in groups. Full details will be posted on Blackboard in Week 2. This oral presentation to be undertaken during the tutorials is a critical, mandatory step toward the course's final assignment. Completing the Pitch is a prerequisite for undertaking the next assignment, Current Affairs Story. Each student will pitch, in class, a current affairs story that one intends to pursue as one's independent project. The pitch must make the case for why the story is compelling and worth producing as audio, and must include: A clear story angle or entry point — not just a topic, but the specific people, scene, or moment that will carry the story. A production plan — who you intend to interview, what access you have, and what sound elements (ambient sound, tape, etc.) you plan to incorporate. A short reflection on the ethical, legal, technological, or cultural considerations relevant to producing and sharing this story — for example, consent, sensitive subject matter, representation of local or community voices, or platform/distribution concerns. Recording of Oral and Practical Assessment All presentations will be recorded for marking purposes via recording facilities available where the assessment takes place (eg. ECHO360, Zoom, camera device) Recordings will be retained by the School of Communication and Arts for at least 12 months from the release of the final grade for the course. Recordings will be stored in a secure manner and will only be accessed by authorised school staff for the purposes of: Moderation of marking; Provision of feedback to the student(s) recorded; and/or Re-marking following a successful re-mark application. assessment_details.title: Current Affairs Story
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Students will undertake this assignment independently and after completing the previous assignment, Pitch: Current Affairs Story. Full details will be available via Blackboard in Week 2. Using what they have learned this semester, each student will be required to script, source, produce and edit a short-form audio current affairs story. The audio story should be between 3-6 minutes. One should also submit the script (however, it is not necessary for the script to match the final cut if minor changes were made to the final product during the editing process). The story should address a social issue. This could take the form of a deep dive into a personal experience, a profile, or a broader look at how a group of people responds to an event or issue. Each student should use what they have learned about storytelling and their chosen medium to draw listeners into the narrative world through insightful use of sound elements/effects. One must also incorporate at least one short interview with a source (no more than two sources total is recommended). When submitting your story, one should suggest a potential publication venue, e.g., ABC, Vice or quality podcasts. Students will have the opportunity to workshop their concept, script and final product in the final tutorials. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1 Lecture: Introduction What audio journalism entails, the use of radio and podcast platforms in audio production, and its application today.
Week 1 Tutorial: NO TUTORIALS This week, students undertake individual preparations for the course, e.g., downloading and installing Adobe Suite on their devices.
Week 2 Lecture: Sound storytelling The fundamentals of audio reporting: researching, field/desk work, writing, editing, producing and presenting.
Week 2 Tutorial: Pitching audio news story Identifying newsworthy audio stories and how to craft, develop and plan news stories for radio broadcasts and podcasts.
Week 3 Lecture: Audio production The audio production set-up: What it entails to produce radio and broadcast news using professional studio and field recording equipment.
Week 3 Tutorial: NO TUTORIALS Organised tour of the Media and Production Support (MaPS) department. Also, this week, groups prepare news story pitches for Group Assignment I. Learning outcomes: L05
Week 4 Lecture: Writing for the ear What it means to 'write for the ear’; field-gathering techniques, finding sources, researching story ideas, and witnessing or observing.
Week 4 Tutorial: News/script writing The elements of an audio news story and how to write effectively for sound and delivery.
Week 5 Lecture: Sound gathering Applying the elements of audio in a news story and how to use sound and one’s voice to tell a compelling story.
Week 5 Tutorial: Sound design Field and studio recording in high-quality form, writing, editing as well as mixing techniques. Use of Adobe Audition for creating, editing, and mixing.
Week 6 Lecture: The story structure The editor’s role in audio production and understanding the ‘power’ of sound and its effect on audiences.
Week 6 Tutorial: Editing audio story Developing compelling scenes and soundscapes in audio reporting; understanding narrative structure and styles.
Week 7 Lecture: The audio interview The ‘reporter interview’ in audio storytelling and basics of interviewing in audio journalism.
Week 7 Tutorial: Interviewing How to plan, execute and draw insights from interviews in audio storytelling.
Week 8 Lecture: Podcast-making How the podcast compares to traditional radio broadcast formats and its application in audio production.
Week 8 Tutorial: Hosting and newscasting The application of podcast techniques in audio storytelling and documentary production.
Week 9 Lecture: The audio storyteller Understanding the place and role of the reporter in the audio story.
Week 9 Tutorial: Independent Project Overview Pitch your independent story and receive feedback from the instructors and class.
MID-SEMESTER BREAK - NO LECTURE OR TUTORIALS
Week 10 Lecture: Multi-platform reporting Utilising multimedia elements to enhance audio storytelling and multiplatform reporting.
Week 10 Tutorial: Audio documentary Employing different platforms and strategies e.g., Mobile Journalism (MoJo) to produce compelling long-form stories.

Week 11 Lecture: Ethics and other considerations Ethical values and principles in audio storytelling; media legal, cultural and other accountability concerns in audio journalism. Learning outcomes: L03, L04
Week 11 Tutorial: Critiquing sound and stories A critical look at audio practice and news stories; basics in verification, fact-checking and source criticism.
Week 12 Lecture: Trends in audio journalism New technological and cultural trends in audio journalism, local (and global) issues.
Week 12 Tutorial: Local(ising) sound storytelling Local production, engaging community and employing local assets to amplify voices.
Week 13 Lecture: NO LECTURE
Week 13 Tutorial: Independent Project Update Workshopping students’ audio stories and final independent projects.

Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct.
